implementation_notes: The idiomatic Python guard is a decorator factory - @authorize(policy, Action.READ) wrapping the resource operation - with the policy as a plain class or callable whose decide(ctx, action, resource) returns a small decision object; functools.wraps preserves the wrapped function's identity, and denial raises a dedicated exception that one handler maps to a response. Django and Django REST Framework express the same split as permission_required / LoginRequiredMiddleware or a DRF permission_classes entry: the framework supplies the guard plumbing while the policy stays your object. What replaces the classic structure: decorators and framework permission hooks replace the Guard object; the classic form is still justified for libraries that must stay framework-free or where a single wrapper covers many resources with shared state.
idiom_name: guard decorator over a pure policy callable
pitfalls: A wrapper that swallows the exception or returns None on denial fails open; raise a dedicated exception and let exactly one handler turn it into 403.

Policy instances are module-level state: if the rule source (database, feature flags) changes, every process must see the change consistently - mutate through an owner with locking or keep the policy immutable.
An async view needs an async-aware wrapper (or the check placed inside the ASGI stack); a synchronous decorator around a coroutine returns an un-awaited coroutine instead of enforcing anything.
